precedence_statements.statement: Suno documents the purpose of its controls, but it does not provide creators with one universal public hierarchy guaranteeing which field will always win whenever instructions compete.
Do Not Assume One Field Automatically Overrides the Others
Treat the fields as cooperating influences—not courtroom orders where one command automatically overrules every other command.
Repeating an Instruction Does Not Necessarily Make It Stronger
The Lyrics field is not neutral
Style defines the broad sound world. Lyrics carries words, section labels and local cues. Exclude removes meaningful conflicts.
Personalization influences identity and preference, but it does not replace clear song direction.
Explicit Style field descriptors still override My Taste preferences - Creative Sliders still function independently - Persona Voices and Voice Cloning are unaffected.
Exclude is model guidance, not a hard rule.

When Exclude fails, the likely cause is that 'The positive style strongly implies it' — the fix being to 'Remove the conflicting positive term and add a replacement.' (i.e. the positive Style term effectively out-weighs the Exclude field)
Suno reads both boxes at the same time. If they conflict, the output tries to satisfy both and fails at both.
Put your strongest line first in every section. Suno gives the most melodic weight to the opening line of each tagged section.

Clear the Style Prompt or add 'End' to the style description (given as the fix for when the [End] lyric tag alone fails to stop the song — a concrete case of the lyric bracket being insufficient without style-field support)

rule_block_prompting.observation: Worked example of a Style-vs-Lyrics conflict built on bracket blocks: Style says 'Restrained male solo vocal with no choir' while the Lyrics field contains '[Huge Gospel Chorus]' and '[Full Choir Enters]'. The guide's verdict is that these directly conflict and the lyric brackets actively shape phrasing and vocal density regardless of the style field's negation.

Direct warning against the all-caps emphatic rule-block habit: capitals and repetition such as 'NO CHOIR. ABSOLUTELY NO CHOIR.' do not strengthen a command when competing instructions elsewhere pull toward the unwanted result.

Guidance runs AGAINST catch-all rule blocks: 'Best practice is to shorten the bracket, remove sentence-like wording and place one concise cue directly before the intended event.' Evidence favors specific targeted tags over broad instruction containers.

Mechanism claim underpinning why rule blocks are even attempted: 'Commands in the lyrics box require brackets. Without them, the AI will attempt to sing your instructions as lyrics.' — anything inside [ ] is read as a cue and not sung. This is the stated reason [PERFORMANCE RULES]-type blocks are 'safe' to include, though not evidence they are obeyed.

Countervailing caution on long bracket text: 'Use the tag as a header, then write clean lyric lines underneath it, rather than putting full lyric lines inside brackets, which can cause Suno to sing command text.' Directly at odds with the multi-line [PERFORMANCE RULES] bullet-block form.

NEGATIVE FINDING, stated plainly: across every guide reached in this lane, I found NO source that teaches, names, or demonstrates the '[PERFORMANCE RULES] + bullet list inside lyrics' pattern seen in the known example nrhqq4oreDlBEabw. Jack Righteous's own meta-tags guide 'contains no performance rules or rule-block syntax for lyrics'. The pattern appears to be idiosyncratic to the track author rather than a taught technique, and I found no demonstration that it works.

notes: BIGGEST CAVEAT: this lane returned essentially zero A_demo evidence. Only one instance carries a resolving audio URL, and even there I could not hear the audio or read the song page's real fields — the style/bracket text is quoted from the author's prose about his own track. Everything else is B_recited. No source anywhere demonstrated the pattern with both fields visible AND playable audio side by side.

The single strongest hit for the hunted pattern is one sentence in Jack Righteous's spoken-narration workflow guide that prescribes the lyric label and the style prose together. That is genuine co-declaration advice, verbatim, and it is the centerpiece of this lane's return.

STRUCTURAL FINDING worth flagging: the guide literature actively pushes AGAINST co-declaration. The dominant taught doctrine is strict field separation ('put it in its proper field once'), with explicit warnings that repetition does not strengthen an instruction. The confirmed example nrhqq4oreDlBEabw is therefore NOT the mainstream technique — it is an outlier practice by one creator. Any claim that co-declaration is standard or recommended would be unsupported by what I found.

AUTHORSHIP CONVERGENCE: nrhqq4oreDlBEabw resolves to 'Righteous Report Ep 3 by Jack Righteous', and every substantive co-declaration/precedence source in this lane is also Jack Righteous. The evidence base is close to single-author, so it should be treated as one creator's house style rather than independent corroboration.

PRECEDENCE, honest bottom line: no source states a hard rule, and the best source explicitly denies one exists ('it does not provide creators with one universal public hierarchy'). The only near-precedence claims are (a) positive Style terms effectively beat the Exclude field, and (b) lyric brackets are 'not neutral' and can defeat a style-field negation. Both are third-party inference, not documented behavior.

The [PERFORMANCE RULES] bullet-block form is undocumented and untaught as far as this search reached — and the closest adjacent advice argues against it (keep brackets short, one concise cue, avoid sentence-like wording). Treat it as unvalidated.
Reddit — the most likely home of the rule-block folklore — was inaccessible, so the negative finding on rule blocks is bounded by that gap rather than conclusive.
